title: CodeQuest learning curriculum
status: 103 authored lessons and original projects; browser checks plus explicit local and Apple-toolchain steps where required.
audience: One beginner learner, with intermediate and advanced progression

assistant.role: Optional clarification, hints, and step-by-step explanation
assistant.grading: Code runner checks behavior; assistant feedback is supplementary

level_definitions.beginner: Follow small, clear steps; predict simple outcomes; make a small working project.
level_definitions.intermediate: Combine familiar ideas, handle varied inputs, and debug with less guidance.
level_definitions.advanced: Design, test, and improve larger systems; reason about failure cases, correctness, and performance.

react: JavaScript functions, objects, arrays, events, and async basics

math_policy: Introduce math only when useful to the coding task. Diagnose coding and math understanding separately. Reuse easier math when appropriate; never require higher-level math than the coding unit. Offer short prerequisite refreshers without resetting coding progress.
progress_policy: Track viewed, attempted, completed with help, completed independently, and mastered through a later transfer task separately. Hints and retries remain available.

teaching_style.language: Informal, conversational, plain, and concrete. Explain things as if sitting beside the learner. Introduce unfamiliar terms beside familiar examples.
teaching_style.analogy_preference: Use familiar everyday objects, games, or childhood activities chosen by the learner. Do not assume particular childhood experiences.
sequence: Connect the idea to one familiar thing.
Give the real term and its plain meaning.
Show a small code example or an interactive demonstration.
Explain a relevant limit of the analogy when it matters.
Ask the learner to predict, change, or build one small thing.
teaching_style.accuracy: Analogies support understanding; they are not literal descriptions of computer memory or universal language behavior. State language-specific behavior when relevant.
teaching_style.interaction: Let the learner open a term explanation, ask for a different analogy, inspect a real example, and practice it in the project.
avoid: Multiple new analogies for one idea at the same time
Assuming that a childhood activity is familiar
Showing a metaphor without connecting it to working code

analogy_glossary.analogy: A labeled box for a value.
analogy_glossary.plain_meaning: A name your program uses to refer to a value.
analogy_glossary.connection: greeting is the label; "Hello!" is the text value. In this JavaScript declaration, = gives the name its starting value. It does not ask whether two values match.
analogy_glossary.limit: This helps with text and numbers. Two names can refer to the same object, so they do not always hold separate copies. Some ways of declaring a name let you replace its value; others do not.

analogy_glossary.analogy: A note with a message written on it.
analogy_glossary.plain_meaning: A text value, such as a name or message.
analogy_glossary.connection: The quotation marks mark the text in this code; they are not part of the resulting message.
analogy_glossary.limit: Strings can also contain spaces, punctuation, and digits. A digit in text is not automatically a number used for arithmetic.

analogy_glossary.plain_meaning: A value that is either true or false.
analogy_glossary.limit: Do not assume true and false are interchangeable with the numbers 1 and 0 in every language.

analogy_glossary.plain_meaning: A collection of values kept in an order.
analogy_glossary.connection: pencil is the first item and paper is the second.
analogy_glossary.limit: The tracks use different names and collection rules. In JavaScript, the first array position is numbered 0; different collection types may have other rules.

analogy_glossary.analogy: A recipe you can use again.
analogy_glossary.plain_meaning: A reusable group of instructions. It can receive values and return a result.
analogy_glossary.connection: The input is like an ingredient; double(3) returns 6.
analogy_glossary.limit: Some functions change something or display a message instead of returning a useful result. Returning a value and printing a value are different actions.

analogy_glossary.analogy: If it rains, take an umbrella.
analogy_glossary.plain_meaning: A check that helps the program choose what to do.
analogy_glossary.connection: The umbrella step runs when isRaining is true.
analogy_glossary.limit: The program follows its actual value and comparison rules. It does not infer the weather or your intention.

analogy_glossary.analogy: Put a label on each item in a packing list.
analogy_glossary.plain_meaning: Repeat instructions for a collection or while a condition holds.
analogy_glossary.connection: The same print step runs once for each supplied item.
analogy_glossary.limit: Different loops stop in different ways. A loop whose stopping condition never becomes satisfied can continue indefinitely.

analogy_glossary.analogy: A character profile with labeled details.
analogy_glossary.plain_meaning: A value that groups related details; the exact rules depend on the language.
analogy_glossary.connection: name and health identify details of this JavaScript object.
analogy_glossary.limit: Two names can refer to the same object. Changing it through one name can affect what is seen through the other.

analogy_glossary.analogy: A menu of requests another system accepts.
analogy_glossary.plain_meaning: An agreed way for software parts to interact.
analogy_glossary.example: Ask a practice service for a list of activities.
analogy_glossary.connection: Your code sends an allowed request and handles the response.
analogy_glossary.limit: APIs are not always internet services. Some requests need permission and some fail. The menu picture does not guarantee a successful response.

analogy_glossary.plain_meaning: A system for storing and retrieving data.
analogy_glossary.example: Store practice entries and retrieve entries for one subject.
analogy_glossary.connection: Named fields help identify the data you want to keep and find.
analogy_glossary.limit: Databases organize information in different ways. The cabinet picture does not explain how records connect, how a group of changes finishes together, or what happens when two people change data at once.
